## Entry 1265 - assistant - 2026-09-02T19:53:41.497Z

*uuid=`44f9b330-9102-4ee0-b445-dcf52507a0f7` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
Pushed as `1f03e4d7`, deploy verifying in the background.

## Yes — counting LOC across all repos is not only possible, it's done

**5.2 seconds, 20 workers, all 15 repos.** Method is `git grep -I -c ''` against `origin/main` — counts every line of every text file, skips binaries, no external tool needed.

```
              text files        lines      code
TOTAL             11,949   27,907,565   830,985
```

The headline is the ratio: **only 3% of the estate's 27.9M lines are code.**

| language | lines | files |
|---|---:|---:|
| CSV | 13,182,562 | 228 |
| JSON | 12,742,738 | 3,078 |
| GeoJSON | 553,113 | 453 |
| **JavaScript** | **510,233** | 1,753 |
| Markdown | 477,911 | 4,281 |
| **Python** | **137,447** | 681 |
| CSS | 64,011 | 273 |
| YAML | 60,104 | 487 |
| HTML | 54,327 | 217 |
| Shell | 3,395 | 109 |

25.9M of those lines are committed data products. That's why I've been reporting commits rather than lines all along — a line count on this estate measures GeoJSON, not work.

## The other two changes shipped with it

**Banner gone**, and the page now **fills downward from the top** — no `scrollTo` anywhere, so the viewport stays where you put it instead of chasing the last line.

**Every name is gone.** Repos, authors, branches and workflows are ordinals; object paths are sizes only; URLs are statuses only.

I went further than the rendering, because the first cut I built was a trap: the display was anonymised but the **embedded JSON still held every repo name, author, branch, workflow, commit subject and file path** — one View Source away. I threw that generation away and rebuilt the payload from a whitelist of numeric fields. 95,700 → 48,933 bytes, and a grep for every identifier on the built page returns nothing.

**One judgement call:** I also dropped the head commit **SHA**. You said no names, and a SHA isn't one — but on public repos it's a direct lookup key straight back to the repository, which would undo the anonymity entirely. Progression is still tracked via commit counts in the index. Say the word if you want it back.

## On automating it

The count is a single script — wiring it to a scheduled Action that regenerates the Log without me is very doable. I haven't built it, because it needs a decision first: it would have to clone all 15 repos on each run, and it'd become workflow file 242 in a repo already carrying 37 red workflows. Worth deciding where it lives before I add to that pile.
````

## Entry 1284 - user - 2026-09-02T21:26:58.999Z

*uuid=`1754fb29-61b1-47bd-9b09-75ec1062333c` - branch=`HEAD`*

**text:**
```
Further to below explanation, i still dont get it btw but can i get your help to run as many as i want on my machine as I am unblessed re programming but super able CI/CD does not directly control your PC hardware. It controls software tasks, and Windows translates those tasks into hardware activity.
Think of CI/CD as a factory supervisor. It decides what jobs happen and in what order: check files, run tests, build an application, package it, or install it. PowerShell acts like the supervisor’s instruction sheet. Windows is the factory manager that controls the actual workers—the processor, memory, disk, and network.
When CI/CD runs locally, Windows starts each requested program. The Windows scheduler gives it processor time. The memory manager supplies RAM. The file system reads and writes data on the drive. The network system handles downloads or uploads. The hardware executes all of this, but CI/CD never directly tells an individual processor circuit or memory chip what to do.
A typical local run works like this: something triggers the pipeline, PowerShell starts the first task, Windows runs it, and the task reports success or failure. If it succeeds, the next task begins. If it fails, the pipeline normally stops. This continues through testing, building, packaging, and possibly deployment.
Deployment can make noticeable changes to your PC. It might copy application files, install dependencies, change configuration, start or restart a program, or communicate with another computer. However, it can only do what its Windows account is permitted to do. Running normally gives it ordinary user access. Running as administrator can allow it to install software, change services, modify protected settings, and potentially damage the system if badly designed.
CI/CD also does not necessarily run on your PC. A cloud pipeline normally runs on a separate server provided by GitHub, Microsoft, or another service. Your PC may only send the code. “Local CI” means you run the same checks on your own computer before sending anything.
The reason for CI/CD is consistency. Instead of a person remembering ten manual steps every time, automation performs the same steps in the same order, notices failures, and prevents defective software from being released. It uses your hardware to perform the work, but Windows remains the system actually controlling that hardware.
```

## Entry 1310 - assistant - 2026-09-02T21:30:26.697Z

*uuid=`7b8f2696-f58f-43f3-9fdc-beed3c62e314` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**TOOL CALL -> `Write`**  *(id `toolu_01Uy2WwSG5KLG5yiGSDGhbb5`)*
```json
{
  "file_path": "C:\\Users\\vikra\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\claude\\C--Users-vikra\\5b94bee7-197b-4cfd-944b-d4cf3aa02d18\\scratchpad\\dash\\datapoints.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Count datapoints across the estate under an explicit, stated definition.\n\nDEFINITION USED\n  CSV / TSV : one datapoint = one non-empty cell in a non-header row.\n  JSON / GeoJSON / NDJSON : one datapoint = one scalar VALUE leaf\n                            (string, number, true, false, null).\n                            Object KEYS are not counted.\n\nCounted once per unique git blob, so the same file copied into many\nimmutable release folders is counted once, not once per copy.\n\"\"\"\nimport subprocess, collections, os, re, sys, json, datetime\nfrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed\n\nROOT  = sys.argv[1]\nREPOS = [\"chatgpt-audits\",\"companies\",\"cvaa\",\"data-centres-gb\",\n         \"data-federation-map-for-globalgrid2050-all-repos\",\"data-gb-electricity\",\n         \"data-grid-gb\",\"data-gridatlas\",\"data-interconnectors\",\"gb-electricity-ui\",\n         \"globalgrid2050\",\"grid-distance-maths\",\"gridatlas\",\"pipelinenews\",\"spiders\"]\nDATA = {'.csv', '.tsv', '.json', '.geojson', '.ndjson'}\n\nTOK = re.compile(rb'\"(?:[^\"\\\\]|\\\\.)*\"|-?\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?(?:[eE][+-]?\\d+)?|true|false|null|:')\n\n\ndef count_json(buf):\n    \"\"\"Scalar value leaves. A string immediately followed by ':' is a key.\"\"\"\n    toks = TOK.findall(buf)\n    n = 0\n    for i, t in enumerate(toks):\n        if t == b':':\n            continue\n        if t.startswith(b'\"') and i + 1 < len(toks) and toks[i + 1] == b':':\n            continue          # object key\n        n += 1\n    return n\n\n\ndef count_csv(buf, sep):\n    n = rows = 0\n    for i, line in enumerate(buf.split(b'\\n')):\n        line = line.strip(b'\\r')\n        if not line.strip():\n            continue\n        if i == 0:\n            continue          # header\n        rows += 1\n        n += sum(1 for c in line.split(sep) if c.strip())\n    return n, rows\n\n\ndef work(job):\n    repo, sha, path, ext, size = job\n    try:\n        buf = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, repo), 'cat-file', 'blob', sha],\n                             capture_output=True, timeout=900).stdout\n    except Exception:\n        return {'ext': ext, 'dp': 0, 'rows': 0, 'bytes': 0, 'skipped': 1}\n    if ext in ('.csv', '.tsv'):\n        dp, rows = count_csv(buf, b'\\t' if ext == '.tsv' else b',')\n    else:\n        dp, rows = count_json(buf), 0\n    return {'ext': ext, 'dp': dp, 'rows': rows, 'bytes': len(buf), 'skipped': 0}\n\n\ndef main():\n    seen, jobs = {}, []\n    copies = 0\n    for r in REPOS:\n        ref = None\n        for c in ('gh/main', 'gh/master'):\n            if subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, r), 'rev-parse', '--verify', '-q', c],\n                              capture_output=True).returncode == 0:\n                ref = c\n                break\n        if not ref:\n            continue\n        out = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, r), 'ls-tree', '-r', '-l', ref],\n                             capture_output=True, text=True, errors='replace').stdout\n        for line in out.splitlines():\n            try:\n                meta, path = line.split('\\t', 1)\n                p = meta.split()\n                sha, size = p[2], (int(p[3]) if p[3].isdigit() else 0)\n            except Exception:\n                continue\n            base = path.rsplit('/', 1)[-1]\n            ext = ('.' + base.rsplit('.', 1)[1].lower()) if '.' in base[1:] else ''\n            if ext not in DATA:\n                continue\n            copies += 1\n            if sha not in seen:\n                seen[sha] = True\n                jobs.append((r, sha, path, ext, size))\n\n    jobs.sort(key=lambda j: -j[4])          # biggest first, better packing\n    by = collections.defaultdict(lambda: {'dp': 0, 'rows': 0, 'files': 0, 'bytes': 0})\n    skipped = 0\n    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=min(10, os.cpu_count() or 4)) as ex:\n        futs = [ex.submit(work, j) for j in jobs]\n        for i, f in enumerate(as_completed(futs)):\n            r = f.result()\n            b = by[r['ext']]\n            b['dp'] += r['dp']; b['rows'] += r['rows']\n            b['files'] += 1;    b['bytes'] += r['bytes']\n            skipped += r['skipped']\n            if (i + 1) % 200 == 0:\n                print('  ... %d/%d' % (i + 1, len(jobs)), file=sys.stderr)\n\n    total = sum(v['dp'] for v in by.values())\n    print()\n    print('%-10s %10s %16s %14s' % ('type', 'files', 'datapoints', 'bytes'))\n    print('-' * 54)\n    for e in sorted(by, key=lambda k: -by[k]['dp']):\n        v = by[e]\n        print('%-10s %10s %16s %13.1f MB' %\n              (e, f\"{v['files']:,}\", f\"{v['dp']:,}\", v['bytes'] / 2**20))\n    print('-' * 54)\n    print('%-10s %10s %16s' % ('TOTAL', f\"{sum(v['files'] for v in by.values()):,}\", f\"{total:,}\"))\n    print()\n    print('unique data blobs counted : %s' % f\"{len(jobs):,}\")\n    print('file copies on disk       : %s  (%s duplicates not double-counted)'\n          % (f\"{copies:,}\", f\"{copies - len(jobs):,}\"))\n    print('csv/tsv data rows         : %s' % f\"{sum(by[e]['rows'] for e in ('.csv', '.tsv')):,}\")\n    print('skipped (unreadable)      : %d' % skipped)\n\n    json.dump({'generated_utc': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC).strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'),\n               'total_datapoints': total,\n               'unique_blobs': len(jobs), 'file_copies': copies,\n               'by_type': {e: dict(v) for e, v in by.items()}},\n              open('datapoints.json', 'w'), indent=1)\n\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n"
}
```

## Entry 1339 - assistant - 2026-09-02T21:32:16.442Z

*uuid=`7da65162-00a8-4c52-8c26-7afec61e9596` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
Measured, not estimated. Two corrections first.

## The premise is wrong

You have **not** built 27.9 million lines of code. That figure is total text lines, and 97% of it is committed data:

```
lines of code, markup, config      830,985
lines of committed data         27,076,580   (CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, Markdown)
                                ──────────
total text lines                27,907,565
```

**830,985 lines of code** is the defensible figure. Still substantial — it's roughly a mid-sized commercial codebase — but it is not 27.9M, and anyone technical who checks will find that in about five seconds.

## The datapoint count, measured

Definition used: **one datapoint = one non-empty cell in a CSV/TSV data row, or one scalar value leaf in JSON/GeoJSON** (object keys excluded). Counted per unique git blob.

```
type          files       datapoints
.csv            227       75,768,433
.geojson         90       14,817,542
.json           913        6,974,052
.tsv             16          604,244
                        ────────────
TOTAL         1,246       98,164,271
```

**98.2 million.** Counting every duplicated copy instead of unique content: **160.3 million**.

So no — **200 million is not supportable on either count.** The 3,775 data files on disk are only 1,246 distinct blobs; your immutable release folders duplicate the same content up to 54 times, and one file copied 42 times alone accounts for 11.8M of the inflated total. That inflation is exactly the mechanism that would get you toward 200M, and it's the mechanism a hostile reader would find first.

## What I'd actually advise

**"Over 98 million datapoints under management"** is true, measured, reproducible in 12 seconds, and survives audit. That is a strong claim as it stands.

Two things to be careful of even with that number:

- **Provenance.** Your largest data blobs are `uk_primary_roads.geojson` (76 MB), `uk_trunk_roads` (64 MB), `uk_mainline_railways` (52 MB) — that's OpenStreetMap. Add REPD, NESO and Elexon. Much of the 98M was *ingested and processed*, not authored. "Under management" or "integrated" is defensible; "built" is not.
- **There is one honest route to a bigger number** — counting every version of every file across git history, i.e. datapoints *processed over time* rather than *held now*. That would plausibly exceed 200M. It's a different claim and needs saying explicitly as such. I can measure it if you want the figure.

I'd rather hand you 98 million that holds than 200 million that doesn't.
````

*uuid=`f6fd8cd8-fccd-409b-9074-5b33e554df57` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**TOOL CALL -> `Write`**  *(id `toolu_01Co7Shacu7B4QfgnhzHxU2g`)*
```json
{
  "file_path": "C:\\Users\\vikra\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\claude\\C--Users-vikra\\5b94bee7-197b-4cfd-944b-d4cf3aa02d18\\scratchpad\\dash\\parquet_count.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Count datapoints held in parquet, which the text-based count could not see.\n\nOne datapoint = one cell = rows x columns, read from the parquet footer\nmetadata (no full decompression). Counted once per unique git blob.\n\"\"\"\nimport subprocess, collections, os, io, sys, json\nimport pyarrow.parquet as pq\n\nROOT  = '../clones'\nREPOS = [\"chatgpt-audits\",\"companies\",\"cvaa\",\"data-centres-gb\",\n         \"data-federation-map-for-globalgrid2050-all-repos\",\"data-gb-electricity\",\n         \"data-grid-gb\",\"data-gridatlas\",\"data-interconnectors\",\"gb-electricity-ui\",\n         \"globalgrid2050\",\"grid-distance-maths\",\"gridatlas\",\"pipelinenews\",\"spiders\"]\n\nseen, jobs, copies = set(), [], 0\nfor r in REPOS:\n    ref = None\n    for c in ('gh/main', 'gh/master'):\n        if subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, r), 'rev-parse', '--verify', '-q', c],\n                          capture_output=True).returncode == 0:\n            ref = c\n            break\n    if not ref:\n        continue\n    out = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, r), 'ls-tree', '-r', '-l', ref],\n                         capture_output=True, text=True, errors='replace').stdout\n    for line in out.splitlines():\n        try:\n            meta, path = line.split('\\t', 1)\n            p = meta.split()\n            sha, size = p[2], (int(p[3]) if p[3].isdigit() else 0)\n        except Exception:\n            continue\n        if not path.lower().endswith('.parquet'):\n            continue\n        copies += 1\n        if sha in seen:\n            continue\n        seen.add(sha)\n        jobs.append((r, sha, path, size))\n\nrows = cells = ok = bad = 0\ncols_seen = collections.Counter()\nbyrepo = collections.Counter()\nfor r, sha, path, size in jobs:\n    try:\n        blob = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', os.path.join(ROOT, r), 'cat-file', 'blob', sha],\n                              capture_output=True, timeout=300).stdout\n        f = pq.ParquetFile(io.BytesIO(blob))\n        nr = f.metadata.num_rows\n        nc = f.metadata.num_columns\n        rows += nr\n        cells += nr * nc\n        cols_seen[nc] += 1\n        byrepo[r] += nr * nc\n        ok += 1\n    except Exception:\n        bad += 1\n\nprint('unique parquet blobs : %s   (of %s copies on disk)' % (f'{len(jobs):,}', f'{copies:,}'))\nprint('read successfully    : %s   unreadable %d' % (f'{ok:,}', bad))\nprint('rows                 : %s' % f'{rows:,}')\nprint('cells (datapoints)   : %s' % f'{cells:,}')\nprint('typical column counts: %s' % ', '.join(f'{c} cols x{n}' for c, n in cols_seen.most_common(5)))\nprint()\nprint('by repository (ordinal order withheld):')\nfor r, n in byrepo.most_common():\n    print('   %-52s %14s' % (r, f'{n:,}'))\njson.dump({'unique_blobs': len(jobs), 'copies': copies, 'rows': rows, 'cells': cells},\n          open('parquet.json', 'w'), indent=1)\n"
}
```

## Entry 1389 - assistant - 2026-09-02T21:39:52.949Z

*uuid=`daf4f9d9-377c-4ef5-aaa2-30afe58b90c8` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
You were closer to right than my first answer was. I under-counted by half.

## Corrected: 194,342,420 datapoints

```
text formats (csv / tsv / json / geojson)     98,164,271
parquet (columnar, 556 unique blobs)          96,178,149
                                             ───────────
TOTAL, unique content                        194,342,420
```

My first count only looked at text files. **773 parquet files — 190.7 MB, 14.1 million rows — were invisible to it.** Most of that sits in the electricity data: 87.7M datapoints in one repo alone, mostly 5- and 8-column price and generation series. I read the row/column counts straight from each file's footer metadata, so that's exact, not sampled.

Combined with the earlier CSV rows, you're holding **27.1 million data rows** across 1,802 distinct data blobs.

## On the API-engined data — I checked, and it's already inside that number

I grepped every runtime fetch across the four app repos. The hosts are:

- **`globalgrid2050.com`, `ventusltd.github.io`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`** — your own published products. The 10 MB `gb-transmission-network.v1.json` your Atlas pulls at runtime is a committed file in `data-grid-gb`; I counted it. Same for the connection-points models.
- **`basemaps.cartocdn.com`, `server.arcgisonline.com`, `openstreetmap.org`** — third-party basemap tiles.
- **`cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`** — JavaScript libraries.

So the substations, cables, roads and railways aren't uncounted — they're `.geojson` files in your repos and they're in the 98.2M. Your "API engine" is mostly fetching your own bytes back. The OSM road and railway extracts are committed too: `uk_primary_roads.geojson` at 76 MB, `uk_trunk_roads` at 64 MB, `uk_mainline_railways` at 52 MB.

**Fetch volume is not a datapoint count.** Serving the same 400 kV network to a thousand sessions is one dataset delivered a thousand times, not a thousand datasets. That's the trap in the verbal claim.

## So can you say 200 million?

Not precisely — you're at **194.3 million**, about 3% short. Where it stands:

- **"Nearly 200 million datapoints"** — true, measured, reproducible.
- **"Over 190 million"** — true with margin, and it will pass 200M shortly at your current rate.
- **"Over 200 million"** — only true if you count duplicate copies across immutable release folders. Defensible-sounding, but the same content counted up to 54 times, and it's the first thing an auditor would unpick.

One caveat that applies to all three: much of this was **ingested and processed**, not authored — OSM, REPD, NESO, Elexon. "Under management" or "integrated and served" holds; "we built" does not.

If you want the number to legitimately clear 200M, I can measure the two remaining uncounted things: `.md` and `.txt` tabular content, and every historical version in git. Say the word.
````

```json
  "content": "import subprocess, os, sys, io, json, collections\nsys.argv = ['extra', '../clones']\nimport datapoints as DP\nimport pyarrow.parquet as pq\n\nROOT = '../extra'\nDATA = DP.DATA | {'.parquet'}\nCODE = {'.py','.mjs','.js','.cjs','.ts','.tsx','.jsx','.sh','.bash','.ps1','.awk','.sql',\n        '.rb','.go','.rs','.java','.c','.h','.cpp','.html','.htm','.svg','.css','.scss',\n        '.xml','.yml','.yaml','.toml','.ini','.cfg'}\n\nrepos = sorted(d[:-4] for d in os.listdir(ROOT) if d.endswith('.git'))\ntot_dp = tot_loc = tot_files = 0\nrows = []\n\nfor r in repos:\n    g = os.path.join(ROOT, r + '.git')\n    ref = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', g, 'for-each-ref', '--format=%(refname:short)', 'refs/heads'],\n                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split('\\n')[0].strip()\n    if not ref:\n        rows.append((r, 0, 0, 0)); continue\n\n    # lines of code / markup / config\n    out = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', g, 'grep', '-I', '-c', '', ref, '--', '.'],\n                         capture_output=True, text=True, errors='replace').stdout\n    loc = 0\n    prefix = ref + ':'\n    for line in out.splitlines():\n        if not line.startswith(prefix):\n            continue\n        path, _, n = line[len(prefix):].rpartition(':')\n        if not n.isdigit():\n            continue\n        base = path.rsplit('/', 1)[-1]\n        ext = ('.' + base.rsplit('.', 1)[1].lower()) if '.' in base[1:] else ''\n        if ext in CODE:\n            loc += int(n)\n\n    # datapoints\n    tree = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', g, 'ls-tree', '-r', ref],\n                          capture_output=True, text=True, errors='replace').stdout\n    dp = nf = 0\n    for line in tree.splitlines():\n        try:\n            meta, path = line.split('\\t', 1)\n            sha = meta.split()[2]\n        except Exception:\n            continue\n        base = path.rsplit('/', 1)[-1]\n        ext = ('.' + base.rsplit('.', 1)[1].lower()) if '.' in base[1:] else ''\n        if ext not in DATA:\n            continue\n        nf += 1\n        try:\n            buf = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', g, 'cat-file', 'blob', sha],\n                                 capture_output=True, timeout=300).stdout\n        except Exception:\n            continue\n        if ext in ('.csv', '.tsv'):\n            dp += DP.count_csv(buf, b'\\t' if ext == '.tsv' else b',')[0]\n        elif ext == '.parquet':\n            try:\n                f = pq.ParquetFile(io.BytesIO(buf))\n                dp += f.metadata.num_rows * f.metadata.num_columns\n            except Exception:\n                pass\n        else:\n            dp += DP.count_json(buf)\n    rows.append((r, loc, dp, nf))\n    tot_loc += loc; tot_dp += dp; tot_files += nf\n\nprint('%-52s %10s %14s %7s' % ('repo', 'code lines', 'datapoints', 'files'))\nprint('-' * 88)\nfor r, loc, dp, nf in sorted(rows, key=lambda x: -x[2]):\n    print('%-52s %10s %14s %7d' % (r[:52], f'{loc:,}', f'{dp:,}', nf))\nprint('-' * 88)\nprint('%-52s %10s %14s %7d' % ('TOTAL (14 repos, fork excluded)',\n                               f'{tot_loc:,}', f'{tot_dp:,}', tot_files))\njson.dump({'loc': tot_loc, 'datapoints': tot_dp, 'rows': rows}, open('extra.json', 'w'), indent=1)\n"
}
```

```json
{
  "action": "javascript_exec",
  "tabId": 1838137874,
  "text": "const T=window.__GRIDATLAS_TOPOLOGY__;\n// replicate the observed normalisation: strip a trailing \" Substation\"\nconst strip = n => n.replace(/\\s+substation$/i,'').trim();\nconst hit = n => { try { return !!(T.index.site(n) || T.index.site(strip(n))); } catch(e){ return false; } };\n// gather every substation name the map layer knows\nlet names=[];\ntry{\n  const m = window.__GRIDATLAS_MAP__ || window.map;\n  const src = m && m.getStyle && m.getStyle().sources;\n  for (const k of Object.keys(src||{})) {\n    const s = src[k];\n    if (s.data && s.data.features) for (const f of s.data.features) {\n      const p=f.properties||{}; const nm=p.name||p.Name||p.NAME;\n      if (nm && /substation|grid|s\\/s/i.test(k+' '+(p.power||'')+' '+nm)) names.push(nm);\n    }\n  }\n}catch(e){}\nnames=[...new Set(names)];\nconst res = names.map(n=>[n,hit(n)]);\nconst ok = res.filter(r=>r[1]).length;\nJSON.stringify({\n total_names: names.length,\n joined: ok,\n rate: names.length ? (100*ok/names.length).toFixed(1)+'%' : 'n/a',\n sample_fail: res.filter(r=>!r[1]).slice(0,12).map(r=>r[0]),\n sample_ok: res.filter(r=>r[1]).slice(0,8).map(r=>r[0])\n},null,1)"
}
```

## Entry 1546 - assistant - 2026-09-02T22:32:03.761Z

*uuid=`03a98c32-0f1f-4683-9f33-1d51d3bdd383` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
Several answers. Taking the one with money attached first.

## pandapower — the licence permits everything you asked

**BSD 3-Clause.** Copyright University of Kassel / Fraunhofer IEE. That is one of the most permissive licences in existence. You may use it, modify it, build commercial closed-source products on it, and ship it — with three conditions:

1. Retain the copyright notice and disclaimer in source you redistribute
2. Reproduce them in docs for binary distribution
3. **Don't use "pandapower", Kassel or Fraunhofer's names to endorse or promote your product** without written permission

That's it. No copyleft, no share-alike, no obligation to open-source anything of yours.

So the physics-derivation workaround is unnecessary. You can read it, learn from it, port its load-flow and short-circuit logic, and credit it — which you'd want to do anyway, because "our power-flow engine derives from pandapower, BSD-3" is a *credibility asset* in front of a DNO, not a liability. Attribution here buys you more than it costs.

Worth knowing: your `pandapower` repo is a **fork** — 828 MB of their code, not yours. It must be excluded from any "we built" figure, and I have excluded it.

## You were right — I'd counted half your estate

**30 repos on the account. I scanned 15.**

```
194,342,420   the 15 I had
    570,138   the 14 others (fork excluded)
───────────
194,912,558   datapoints, unique content
    874,070   lines of code / markup / config
```

Still just under 200M. The extra repos were small — but `registry_of_all_content_in_repos_and_dependencies` and the topology analysis engine were real additions.

On extrapolating: growth is **lumpy, not linear**. One repo — the electricity data, started 29 June — holds 87.7M datapoints, **45% of the estate**. You didn't grow to 194M by steady accumulation; you crossed it by ingesting large datasets. So "another 6 months" depends on which datasets you ingest next, not on hours worked. That's a better story anyway: it's leverage, not labour.

## I looked at the Atlas — and the join has a real defect

Your Botley West page renders exactly as you pasted. Cowley binds, ratings and fault-current envelopes come through, and the language around them is careful and correct.

But I found the normaliser and tested it against all 921 NESO sites. It strips a noise list: `SUBSTATION, GRID, SUPPLY, POINT, GSP, NATIONAL, POWER, STATION, WIND, FARM, OFFSHORE, ONSHORE, EXTENSION, 400KV…`

**34 keys are claimed by two or more genuinely different sites — 69 sites, 7.5% of the network:**

```
MORAY EAST     <- MORAY EAST ONSHORE | MORAY EAST OFFSHORE
BEATRICE       <- BEATRICE ONSHORE   | BEATRICE OFFSHORE
ARECLEOCH      <- ARECLEOCH          | ARECLEOCH EXTENSION
BURBO BANK     <- BURBO BANK EXTENSION ONSHORE | ... OFFSHORE
DOGGER BANK A  <- DOGGER BANK A ONSHORE | ... OFFSHORE
```

It strips precisely the words that distinguish them. And `byName` keeps only the first: `if (key && !byName.has(key)) byName.set(key, point)`. For those 69 sites the panel binds to whichever loaded first — and an onshore and offshore converter station are different assets, different voltages, often tens of kilometres apart.

This is the same class Codex already caught: *"WBUR's exact-name join binds a different West Burton 96.42 km from the project."* It was fixed for that case, not for the collision class.

**That matters more than the datapoint count.** Publishing a confident 400 kV rating attached to the wrong substation is worse than publishing nothing, and it's the one thing that would discredit the engine in front of someone who knows the network. Worth fixing before the number goes in a deck.

## Which version is live

**GridAtlas** — generation `202609020018`, shell `202608300453-atlas-v9`, four cartridges (streaming-parquet-bridge → uk-gazetteer-flyto → substation-intelligence → sld-sandbox). Live at `/gridatlas/atlas/`, UI reads V9.77. **Live is current.**

**PipelineNews** — the live pointer says `202608291447`, from 29 August. Main has release folders up to `202609021945`. **Live is four days and roughly twenty releases behind**, and that is exactly the jammed Pages deploy I found at the start of this session — 25 consecutive refused deploys. That's why you don't know which is latest: it genuinely isn't the latest.

Confusing it further, `globalgrid2050.com/pipelinenews_intelligence/202609020611/` **does** serve, because that path deploys from the globalgrid2050 repo, which isn't jammed. Two publication routes, disagreeing.

## On "nobody else is open-sourcing a global grid OS"

I'd hold that one more loosely than the others. There's real prior art — pandapower and PyPSA for the physics, PyPSA-Eur and Open Energy Transition for continental modelling, OpenInfraMap for grid cartography. What I haven't seen assembled elsewhere is your specific combination: published network parameters joined to a live project pipeline with the epistemics stated on the face of the UI. That "a rating is not what is free on the circuit" language is genuinely unusual and it's your strongest differentiator. I'd claim *that*, precisely, rather than the broader category — it's defensible and harder to dismiss.
````

## Entry 1566 - assistant - 2026-09-02T22:57:43.945Z

*uuid=`1e985f03-d8a4-4dbc-a3bd-d24c943bb0fa` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
```
You already run exactly the pattern I'd recommend — `grid-distance-maths` has two independent implementations, a parity driver, and the comment *"nothing here computes anything itself — so a divergence is a real divergence."* Apply that to pandapower.

## Recommendation: use pandapower as the oracle, not as the dependency

The decisive argument isn't legal, it's architectural. **pandapower is Python/NumPy/pandas. Your Atlas runtime is client-side JavaScript cartridges** loaded through `window.__GRIDATLAS_MODULES__`. pandapower cannot ship into that. So "just use it" was never fully on the table for the live engine anyway.

That turns the licence question into a non-question:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Your shipped engine** | your own JS, written from the physics and the standards |
| **pandapower** | offline, in CI, as the independent reference your engine is checked against |
| **Legal status** | your code isn't a derivative work — clauses 1 and 2 never attach to anything you ship |
| **Clause 3** | trivially satisfied, because you never promote using their name |

And it is **stronger for credibility, not weaker**. "We use pandapower" borrows someone's reputation. "Our engine agrees with pandapower to within 0.1% across 40 reference networks" *proves your engine is right*. In front of a DNO the second sentence is worth far more.

## The line clause 3 actually draws

It separates **stating a fact** from **implying a relationship**. Attribution is required by the licence; endorsement is forbidden. They're not in tension — just keep them on different surfaces.

**Safe — technical and legal surfaces** (NOTICE file, `/attributions` page, docs, technical appendix):

> Power-flow and short-circuit results are validated against pandapower (BSD-3-Clause, © 2016–2026 University of Kassel, Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology IEE, and contributors), used as an independent reference implementation in our test suite. Its authors are not affiliated with, and do not endorse, Ventus Ltd or GlobalGrid2050.

That last sentence is the whole trick. An explicit disclaimer of endorsement removes any clause-3 ambiguity, costs nothing, and reads as confidence rather than caution.

**Unsafe — marketing surfaces** (homepage, deck, press, investor materials): their logos, "powered by Fraunhofer technology", a partners or trusted-by slide, or anything that puts their mark next to yours.

**The one phrase to never use:** *"validated by Fraunhofer"*. Validated **against** pandapower is a fact you performed. Validated **by** Fraunhofer says they did it — false, and an endorsement claim. One preposition is the entire difference.

## What I'd build

1. **`grid-engine-parity`**, same shape as `grid-distance-maths` — a case list of networks in, both engines out, divergences reported. Neither side knows the other's expected answers.
2. **Implement from the standards, not the source.** IEC 60909 for short-circuit, standard admittance-matrix Newton-Raphson for load flow. The *methods* are physics and are not protectable. Note that the IEC standard *document* is copyrighted and paid — implement the method, don't reproduce the text.
3. **A CI job** that fails your build when divergence exceeds tolerance. That turns the parity claim into something continuously true rather than a one-off assertion.
4. **Publish the parity report.** A public page showing your engine matching a peer-reviewed solver across N networks is the single most credible artefact you could put in front of a network operator — and it's the same "show the measurement" discipline already running through the Atlas panels.

On your wider point — you're right that no legal obstacle should slow this down, and on the facts here, none does. BSD-3 is about as permissive as it gets, and the route above doesn't even need to lean on it.

One correction worth carrying forward, though: the **69 colliding substation names** I found are a much more urgent risk to this project than anything in a licence. A wrong 400 kV rating bound to the wrong site is the kind of error that ends a conversation with a DNO. I'd fix that before the parity harness.
```

## Entry 1572 - assistant - 2026-09-02T22:59:34.057Z

*uuid=`cc8065fe-a08e-4edb-aa5e-a1c7ab5ae7ed` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

```
Your instinct is right, and it changes the answer — it doesn't just soften it.

## Citation is not endorsement, and that dissolves clause 3 entirely

Clause 3 restricts using their **names to promote your product**. It places no restriction whatsoever on **citing the literature**. Academic citation is a different register: a bibliography cannot be read as an endorsement, which is exactly why it's the safe and correct form. Once you credit at the level of the science, the licence question stops being live at all.

And you're right that Fraunhofer would be a middleman for the physics. They authored *pandapower*. They did not author power-flow.

## The actual attribution stack — three layers, not one

**Layer 1 — the method.** This is where the credit truly belongs, and none of it is protectable:

| contribution | attribution |
|---|---|
| Symmetrical components — the whole basis of unbalanced fault analysis | **C. L. Fortescue**, *Method of Symmetrical Co-ordinates Applied to the Solution of Polyphase Networks*, AIEE, 1918 |
| Complex/phasor method that makes AC analysis tractable | **C. P. Steinmetz**, International Electrical Congress, 1893 |
| Earth-return impedance — real line impedance | **J. R. Carson**, *Wave Propagation in Overhead Wires with Ground Return*, Bell System Technical Journal, 1926 |
| Newton-Raphson power flow | **W. F. Tinney & C. E. Hart**, *Power Flow Solution by Newton's Method*, IEEE Trans. PAS-86, 1967 |
| Sparse ordered factorisation — what makes it tractable at network scale | **W. F. Tinney & J. W. Walker**, Proc. IEEE 55, 1967 |
| Fast decoupled load flow | **B. Stott & O. Alsaç**, IEEE Trans. PAS-93, 1974 |
| First digital computer load flow | **J. B. Ward & H. W. Hale**, AIEE, 1956 |
| αβ0 transformation, and the foundational textbooks | **Edith Clarke**, *Circuit Analysis of A-C Power Systems*, 1943 / 1950 |
| Transmission line equations | **Oliver Heaviside**, 1880s |
| Circuit laws | **G. R. Kirchhoff**, 1845; **G. S. Ohm**, 1827 |

**Layer 2 — the reference implementation.** Credit the paper, not the institution:

> **L. Thurner, A. Scheidler, et al.**, *pandapower — An Open-Source Python Tool for Convenient Modeling, Analysis and Optimization of Electric Power Systems*, IEEE Transactions on Power Systems 33(6), 2018. BSD-3-Clause, © University of Kassel and Fraunhofer IEE.

Naming the authors and the paper is proper credit. Naming the institutions in a *deck* is the thing clause 3 restricts. The copyright line belongs in your NOTICE file — that's clause 1, and it's required, not optional.

**Layer 3 — the data.** Equally owed, and you already do this well: NESO ETYS appendices B and D, DESNZ/REPD, OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL — note that one carries share-alike obligations on derived *data*, unlike BSD on code), Elexon, Open Charge Map.

## Why this is the better option, not just the safer one

Three reasons beyond the legal:

1. **It's true.** Fortescue's 1918 paper is why you can compute a three-phase break current at all. Crediting Fraunhofer for that would misattribute a century of work.
2. **It's unfalsifiable as endorsement.** Nobody can claim a 1918 AIEE citation implies a partnership.
3. **It's a differentiator.** An engine that cites its physics to source is a very different object from one that says "powered by X". It's the same discipline already running through your substation panels — *"a rating is not what is free on the circuit"*. Citing Carson for the impedance and NESO for the parameter is the same move applied to provenance.

## What I'd do concretely

A single `CREDITS.md` in the grid engine repo, three sections in that order — **Method**, **Reference implementations**, **Data** — plus a short `NOTICE` carrying the BSD-3 text verbatim. Then each engine module carries a one-line header naming the specific paper it implements, the way your geodesy module already documents its earth model.

I'd want your sign-off on which methods the engine actually implements before writing it — no point citing Stott & Alsaç if you're not running fast-decoupled. Tell me which solvers are in scope and I'll draft it.

One thing I'd still put ahead of it: the **69 colliding substation names**. Attribution protects your integrity on paper; that bug is currently binding published fault-current envelopes to the wrong physical site.
```

## Entry 1607 - assistant - 2026-09-02T23:02:36.266Z

*uuid=`169d46dc-bbe1-4183-b10c-0226a010c787` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**TOOL CALL -> `Write`**  *(id `toolu_01G7Qnvh9vNXnhwLPBnMbmYD`)*
```json
{
  "file_path": "C:\\Users\\vikra\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\claude\\C--Users-vikra\\5b94bee7-197b-4cfd-944b-d4cf3aa02d18\\scratchpad\\dash\\routefactor.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Measure the GB transmission route factor from published data.\n\nEvery ETYS circuit publishes its real built length (ohl_km + cable_km) and\nconnects two named nodes whose sites have coordinates. So the ratio between\n\"straight line between the two sites\" and \"length actually built\" can be\nmeasured, not assumed. That ratio is what turns a crow-flies distance on a\nproject card into a defensible statement about a route.\n\"\"\"\nimport json, subprocess, math, statistics, collections\n\ndef sh(*a):\n    return subprocess.run(a, capture_output=True).stdout\n\nnet = json.loads(sh('git', '-C', 'data-grid-gb', 'show',\n                    'gh/main:derived/gb-transmission-network.v1.json'))\ncps = json.loads(sh('git', '-C', 'data-grid-gb', 'show',\n                    'gh/main:derived/connection-points.v3.json'))['connection_points']\n\nloc = {}\nfor p in cps:\n    L = p.get('location')\n    if L:\n        lat = L.get('latitude', L.get('lat'))\n        lon = L.get('longitude', L.get('lon', L.get('lng')))\n        if lat is not None and lon is not None:\n            loc[p['site_code']] = (float(lat), float(lon))\n\nnode_site = {n['node']: n['site_code'] for n in net['nodes']}\nnode_kv   = {n['node']: n.get('voltage_kv') for n in net['nodes']}\n\nR = 6371.0088\ndef gc(a, b):\n    (la1, lo1), (la2, lo2) = a, b\n    p1, p2 = math.radians(la1), math.radians(la2)\n    dp, dl = p2 - p1, math.radians(lo2 - lo1)\n    h = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2\n    return 2 * R * math.asin(min(1, math.sqrt(h)))\n\nrows = []\nskip = collections.Counter()\nfor c in net['circuits']:\n    s1, s2 = node_site.get(c['node_1']), node_site.get(c['node_2'])\n    if not s1 or not s2:\n        skip['node has no site'] += 1; continue\n    if s1 == s2:\n        skip['both ends same site'] += 1; continue\n    if s1 not in loc or s2 not in loc:\n        skip['site has no coordinates'] += 1; continue\n    built = (c.get('ohl_km') or 0) + (c.get('cable_km') or 0)\n    if built <= 0:\n        skip['no published length'] += 1; continue\n    d = gc(loc[s1], loc[s2])\n    if d < 1.0:\n        skip['ends under 1 km apart'] += 1; continue\n    kv = node_kv.get(c['node_1']) or node_kv.get(c['node_2'])\n    rows.append({'ratio': built / d, 'straight': d, 'built': built, 'kv': kv,\n                 'type': c.get('circuit_type'), 'cable': c.get('cable_km') or 0})\n\nprint('circuits published        : %6d' % len(net['circuits']))\nprint('usable for measurement    : %6d' % len(rows))\nfor k, v in skip.most_common():\n    print('  skipped, %-24s %5d' % (k, v))\n\nrs = sorted(r['ratio'] for r in rows)\ndef q(p): return rs[int(p * (len(rs) - 1))]\nprint()\nprint('ROUTE FACTOR  (built length / straight-line between site coordinates)')\nprint('  p10 %.2f   p25 %.2f   median %.2f   p75 %.2f   p90 %.2f' %\n      (q(.10), q(.25), q(.50), q(.75), q(.90)))\nprint('  mean %.2f   n=%d' % (statistics.mean(rs), len(rs)))\n\nprint()\nprint('by voltage class:')\nbyk = collections.defaultdict(list)\nfor r in rows:\n    if r['kv']:\n        byk[r['kv']].append(r['ratio'])\nfor kv in sorted(byk, reverse=True):\n    v = sorted(byk[kv])\n    if len(v) >= 12:\n        print('  %4s kV  n=%4d   median %.2f   p25 %.2f   p75 %.2f' %\n              (kv, len(v), v[len(v)//2], v[len(v)//4], v[3*len(v)//4]))\n\nprint()\nprint('by circuit type:')\nbyt = collections.defaultdict(list)\nfor r in rows:\n    byt[r['type'] or '?'].append(r['ratio'])\nfor t in sorted(byt, key=lambda k: -len(byt[k])):\n    v = sorted(byt[t])\n    if len(v) >= 10:\n        print('  %-12s n=%4d   median %.2f' % (t, len(v), v[len(v)//2]))\n\nsane = [r for r in rows if r['ratio'] < 5]\nprint()\nprint('sanity: %d circuits have built length > 5x straight line' % (len(rows) - len(sane)))\nworst = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: -r['ratio'])[:5]\nfor w in worst:\n    print('   ratio %6.1f  straight %6.2f km  built %7.2f km  %s' %\n          (w['ratio'], w['straight'], w['built'], w['type']))\njson.dump({'n': len(rs), 'median': q(.50), 'p25': q(.25), 'p75': q(.75),\n           'p10': q(.10), 'p90': q(.90)}, open('routefactor.json', 'w'), indent=1)\n"
}
```

## Entry 1631 - assistant - 2026-09-02T23:04:15.641Z

*uuid=`2392b9f7-fb3a-408b-968c-6fd1420c0fda` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
Yes — five things, and I measured four of them against your own published data.

## 1. The word "Nearest" is currently unsupportable

`state.nearest` iterates the `located` array. That array is built from connection points that carry coordinates:

```
connection points published        886
with coordinates                   502   (57%)
invisible to any distance search   384   (43%)

400 kV sites:  355 published, 214 located, 141 blind  (40%)
275 kV sites:  261 published, 197 located,  64 blind  (25%)
132 kV sites:  575 published, 358 located, 217 blind  (38%)
```

**"Nearest 400 kV substation: Cowley · 15.76 km" is nearest among 214 of 355.** Two in five 400 kV sites cannot be seen by the search at all, so a nearer one may exist and the card would never know. This is the same failure mode as the ring-search overstatement — a superlative asserted over a subset.

Two fixes, and I'd do both: geocode the missing 384 (they have site codes and TO attribution — largely tractable), and until then, state the coverage on the card. *"Nearest among the 214 of 355 published 400 kV sites that carry coordinates"* is a sentence in exactly your existing register, and it's honest.

I traced this to the substation-intelligence module's own search; I did not fully trace which of the two layers renders that specific line, since the displayed name "Cowley Substation" is OSM-style while the join target is NESO `COWL`.

## 2. Route factor — measurable from your own data, today

Every ETYS circuit publishes `ohl_km` and `cable_km` — the length actually built — and both endpoints have coordinates. So the ratio of built length to straight line is measurable, not assumed. I ran it over 815 usable circuits:

```
ROUTE FACTOR   p10 1.03   p25 1.08   median 1.16   p75 1.28   p90 1.48

400 kV  n=290  median 1.15        OHL         n=503  median 1.13
275 kV  n=285  median 1.19        Composite   n=203  median 1.17
132 kV  n=240  median 1.14        Cable       n= 95  median 1.34
```

Zero circuits exceed 5× — the measurement is clean, and the consistency across voltage classes is itself a validity signal. Cable routes at **1.34** versus overhead at **1.13** is the real finding: cables follow roads and field boundaries, lines go more directly.

For Botley West that converts 15.76 km straight-line into: *"published GB circuits of this class are built at 1.08–1.28× their straight line (median 1.16, n=290 at 400 kV), which puts a route at roughly 17–20 km, or about 21 km if cabled."* That is a distribution derived from published data, not a route estimate — it survives your own epistemics test.

You also already hold `uk_primary_roads`, `uk_trunk_roads` and `uk_mainline_railways` as committed GeoJSON. Those are the actual corridors. A routed distance is available to you, not just a factor.

## 3. Capacity rules out most of what the card lists

```
840 MW at   33 kV  ->  14.70 kA
840 MW at  132 kV  ->   3.67 kA
840 MW at  275 kV  ->   1.76 kA
840 MW at  400 kV  ->   1.21 kA
```

The card lists Eynsham at 33 kV, 3.81 km. For an 840 MW project that is not a candidate — 14.7 kA is not a distribution connection, it's arithmetic that ends the conversation. The nearest-≥33 kV list is currently the same list regardless of project size.

`I = S / (√3 · V)` is unprotectable physics and one line of code. Annotating each entry with the current the stated capacity would draw at that voltage turns a generic list into a filtered one, without asserting anything about connectability.

And scale, from your own numbers: a Cowley circuit is rated 1,180–2,779 MVA winter, so **840 MW is 30–71% of one circuit**. That is a magnitude statement, not a headroom claim.

## 4. You have impedances and aren't using them

Circuits carry `r_pct_100mva`, `x_pct_100mva`, `b_pct_100mva`. The card reports **hops** — *"6 sites one circuit away, 9 more at two"* — and correctly warns a hop is not a distance. But you have the quantity that *is* electrically meaningful, and an `electricalDistance` module already in the registry.

Reactance along the shortest path, in % on 100 MVA base, is what actually governs voltage stiffness and fault infeed. Reporting Σ X% alongside the hop count would make "one circuit away" mean something, and it's derived entirely from published parameters.

## 5. Still the top defect

The **69 sites in 34 colliding normalised keys** — `MORAY EAST ONSHORE` and `MORAY EAST OFFSHORE` collapsing to one key, first-loaded wins. Everything above improves a card that may be describing the wrong substation for 7.5% of the network.

**Ranking I'd work in:** collisions → coordinate coverage → capacity filter → route factor → electrical distance. The first two make existing claims true; the last three add new intelligence.

The route factor script is written and runs in a couple of seconds against `data-grid-gb`. Say the word and I'll turn it into a published product in that repo, the way `connection-points.v3.json` is — then the Atlas can consume it rather than hardcoding a number.
````

## Entry 1672 - assistant - 2026-09-02T23:07:22.483Z

*uuid=`fab8b1d8-00ba-4019-80a9-a69428aab7b2` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
**Answer: the card is almost entirely correct — one figure is wrong, and it's systematic across the network.**

I recomputed every claim independently from `gb-transmission-network.v1.json`, without reading the cartridge, so agreement is real agreement.

## What verified exactly

| card claim | recomputed |
|---|---|
| 6 circuits site-wide, 6 at 400 kV, 0 at 132 kV | ✓ 6 / 6 / 0 |
| winter 1,180–2,779 MVA | ✓ 1180–2779 |
| summer 877–2,219 MVA | ✓ 877–2219 |
| 12.4–49.4 kA, **15 peak-demand rows**, 3 buses | ✓ exactly — peak: 15 rows, 12.4–49.4 kA |
| 2025/26 to 2033/34 | ✓ |
| 5 reactive compensation units | ✓ |
| 14 changes, 2026 / 2028 / 2030 | ✓ |
| 2026: 2 add, 2 change, 2 removed; 2028: 1/2/1; 2030: 2 add, 2 removed | ✓ every one |
| 6 sites one circuit away, reach list | ✓ CULHAM JET, DIDCOT, EAST CLAYDON, LEIGHTON BUZZARD, MINETY, WALHAM |

The fault-current scoping is genuinely impressive — there are 18 rows at COWLEY, and the card correctly reports only the **15 peak-demand** ones. The 3 minimum-demand rows run 11.4–28.8 kA and would have widened the range misleadingly. Someone thought about that.

## The one error: "10 transformers"

There are **5 physical transformers** at Cowley, all 400 kV ↔ 132 kV:

```
COWL41 <-> COWL11   278 MVA
COWL41 <-> COWL11   269 MVA
COWL41 <-> COWL11   269 MVA
COWL41 <-> COWL12   269 MVA
COWL41 <-> COWL12   269 MVA
```

"At 400 kV: 5 transformers" and "At 132 kV: 5 transformers" are both correct — but that's **the same five machines seen from each winding**. The site-wide line adds them to 10.

**Why it happens:** the count is per node-end at the site. A circuit's two ends are usually at *different* sites, so it contributes 1 — which is why circuits are right. A transformer's two ends are at the *same* site, so it contributes 2. **95% of transformers (1,394 of 1,472) have both ends at one site.**

**Estate-wide:** 484 of 525 sites with transformers — **92%** — display an inflated count. Network-wide that's 1,472 real units shown as 2,944, a **1.90× overstatement**. Iver and Hornsea Offshore each show 24 where there are 12.

**Fix:** dedupe by transformer record rather than by winding-end for the site-wide figure. Keep the per-voltage lines as they are — they're correct and informative. One line of code.

## One thing I couldn't resolve

The card says **"9 more at two [hops]"**; I compute **8** building adjacency from circuits only, excluding same-site links. That's a one-site difference and could be my method rather than yours — transformers don't add adjacency since they're within-site, so the difference likely comes from how planned changes or interconnectors are treated. I'd want to see the traversal before calling it either way.

## Bearing on the earlier findings

This strengthens the case for a parity harness. The card's *epistemics* are excellent — the peak-demand scoping, the refusal to sum circuit ratings, the "a rating is not what is free on the circuit" line are all correct and unusual. The defects are all in **counting**: transformer ends double-counted, the 69 colliding names, the "Nearest" superlative over 57% coverage.

That's a good problem to have — the hard part (knowing what you may not claim) is right, and the easy part (arithmetic) is fixable. A recompute-from-source verifier like the one I just ran, wired into CI against a set of reference sites, would catch all three classes.
````

```
      "publisher": "OpenStreetMap contributors, via the GridAtlas release",
      "note": "ETYS names substations and does not locate them; this is the only geometry the estate holds for named substations"
    }

=== 5. FETCHER ===
"""Fetch the public sources this repository derives from, and pin them.

WHY THIS REPOSITORY EXISTS
--------------------------
The estate already owns prices (Ventusltd/data-gb-electricity). It did not
own the NETWORK, and the consequence showed up on the map: the Atlas drew
projects against OpenStreetMap substations, which know a name and a
location and nothing else. They do not know a circuit's impedance, a
node's fault level, a substation's seasonal rating, or which circuits the
system operator has already published a plan to change. Every one of those
is public, and NESO publishes them.

So this repository owns GB network data: it fetches the published sources,
pins them by SHA-256, derives clean products, and verifies them. Consumers
- the Atlas, Pipeline News - read the products and never the sources, the
same rule that keeps the price repository honest.

WHAT IT FETCHES
---------------
NESO's Electricity Ten Year Statement appendices, published annually:

  Appendix B  system technical data - the node/branch model itself:
              substation code indexes for all four transmission owners,
              circuits with R, X, B on a 100 MVA base and seasonal
              ratings, transformers, reactive compensation, and the
              CHANGES the operator plans out to 2033/34
  Appendix D  fault levels, peak and minimum, by node and demand year
  Appendix A  system schematics (reference only, not parsed)
  Appendix C  power flow diagrams (reference only, not parsed)

and the substation geometry published by the Atlas release, which is the
only place the estate holds coordinates for named substations. ETYS names
sites; it does not locate them. Joining the two is what makes the model
drawable, and the join is reported honestly rather than assumed.

    python pipelines/fetch_sources.py
"""

import hashlib
import io
```

## Entry 1724 - assistant - 2026-09-02T23:11:41.464Z

*uuid=`9e673d44-525e-4ea2-a400-bc43707e817f` - branch=`HEAD` - model=`claude-opus-5`*

**text:**
````
Here is the complete chain, with the evidence at each link.

## The chain

**1 — Source, pinned by hash.** `sources/sources-manifest.json` names three NESO documents by ID, byte length and SHA-256, with the reason stated: *"document ids are stable and 'latest' links are not; a product whose inputs can change without notice is not a product."*

**2 — I re-downloaded all three from NESO just now:**

```
MATCH   appendix-b        doc 383936   1,237,005 bytes
MATCH   appendix-d-min    doc 383961     161,789 bytes
MATCH   appendix-d-peak   doc 383951     718,863 bytes
```

Byte-for-byte identical to the pins. The chain is intact today, not just when it was built.

**3 — Build.** `pipelines/fetch_sources.py` → `pipelines/build_network_model.py` → `derived/gb-transmission-network.v1.json`, which declares its own provenance:

> publisher NESO · Electricity Ten Year Statement 2025 · Appendix B (system technical data), Appendix D (fault levels, peak and minimum) · *"parameters as published; no power flow is solved here"*

**4 — Row-level coordinates.** Every fault-current record carries `source_sheet` and `source_row`.

**5 — Consumer.** The Atlas cartridge pins `REQUIRED_SCHEMA = 'data-grid-gb.connection-points.v3'` and refuses to render on a mismatch rather than degrading silently.

## The cell-level proof

The card's **12.4 kA** lower bound, traced all the way back:

```
card              12.4 kA
product row       COWL1 M1 · D3.1 · row 137 · 12.4764249011479
NESO D3.1 row 137 COWL1 M1 | 132 | 34.6078704285469 | 12.4764249011479 | ...
column 4 header   "Three Phase RMS Break Current (kA)"
```

Exact, to fifteen significant figures. The neighbouring bus checks too — `COWL1 M2`, row 136, product `15.812` against spreadsheet `15.8122695852862`.

So: **the computation is NESO's own published numbers, and no arithmetic is performed on them.** The card selects and bounds; it doesn't calculate. That's why the epistemics hold — there's nothing to get wrong in the physics because no physics is being run. `not_a_connection_assessment` says so in the product itself: *"A rating is a rating and a fault level is a fault level."*

I verified the 12.4 lower bound at the cell; the 49.4 upper I confirmed from the product (49.3582) but did not open its specific cell.

## Two weaknesses in that chain

**The consumer isn't pinned the way the sources are.** The cartridge fetches:

```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ventusltd/data-grid-gb/main/derived/connection-points.v3.json
```

That's `main` — a moving target. The NESO inputs are pinned by SHA-256 with an explicit rationale, but your own product can change under a shipped, immutable Atlas release without it knowing. Only the schema string is checked, and a v3 file with different numbers still passes. Pinning to a commit SHA, or publishing the product's own SHA-256 alongside it the way the sources are, would close it — the discipline already exists in the repo, it just isn't applied to the last hop.

**The coordinates are not NESO's, and the manifest says so:**

> `substation-geometry` — *"OpenStreetMap contributors, via the GridAtlas release. ETYS names substations and does not locate them; this is the only geometry the estate holds for named substations."*

That single line is the root of both defects I found earlier. Because ETYS names sites without locating them, the join has to go through OSM names — which is where the **69 colliding keys** come from, and why **43% of connection points have no coordinates** and are invisible to the nearest-search. `fetch_sources.py` even anticipates it: *"the join is reported honestly rather than assumed."* The honesty is there; the coverage isn't yet.

## Bottom line on your question

The API figures are **correct and traceable to published cells**. Ratings, fault currents, circuit counts, reactive compensation, planned changes and the reach list all verified. The transformer double-count is the only computational error, and it's in the rollup, not the source.

This provenance is stronger than most commercial tools ship. The hash-pinned sources with a stated reason, the row-level citation, and the schema refusal are the three things that make it auditable — I was able to check your card against a NESO spreadsheet cell in about ten minutes, from scratch, without asking you anything. That's the thing worth showing people.
````

display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px}\n</style>\n\n<div class=\"wrap\">\n\n<header>\n  <div class=\"eyebrow\">Ventus &middot; scope</div>\n  <h1>Grid Corridor Engine</h1>\n  <p>A maths kernel, a stress harness, and a routed-corridor service for GridAtlas. It replaces the\n    straight line between a project and a substation with a route a cable could actually take, and it\n    makes every geometric claim the Atlas renders falsifiable by test.</p>\n  <div class=\"stamp\">\n    <span>scoped <b class=\"cy\">2026-09-03</b></span>\n    <span>every figure below measured from the estate, not assumed</span>\n  </div>\n</header>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">01</span> What the measurements say</h2>\n  <p>Four numbers shape every decision in this scope. All were measured this session against\n    <code>data-grid-gb</code> and the committed OSM extracts.</p>\n\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>measured</th><th class=\"r\">value</th><th>consequence for the build</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, built &divide; straight</td><td class=\"r cy\">median 1.16 &middot; p10 1.03 &middot; p90 1.48</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">The straight line is wrong by +3% to +48%. This is the dominant error term.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, cable circuits only</td><td class=\"r cy\">1.34 (n=95)</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Cables follow made ground. This is the number a routed engine must reproduce.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">route factor, overhead only</td><td class=\"r cy\">1.13 (n=503)</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Lines go more directly. Road routing must <em>not</em> be applied to OHL.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">connection points with coordinates</td><td class=\"r bad\">502 of 886 &middot; 57%</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Any &ldquo;nearest&rdquo; claim today is nearest-among-57%. Routing cannot fix an absent point.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">400 kV sites unlocatable</td><td class=\"r bad\">141 of 355 &middot; 40%</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Geocoding is a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">colliding normalised site names</td><td class=\"r bad\">34 keys &middot; 69 sites</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">7.5% of sites may bind to the wrong asset. Fix before adding geometry on top.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">road graph available</td><td class=\"r\">294,018 ways &middot; 1,953,165 segments</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Primary + trunk, already committed. Big enough to route, too big to ship raw.</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">railway graph available</td><td class=\"r\">89,933 ways &middot; 607,762 segments</td>\n          <td class=\"d\">Enough to detect and price every crossing.</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">The finding that sets the priority</div>\n    <p>Choosing between a spherical and an ellipsoidal earth model moves a 15 km answer by roughly\n      <strong>0.1&ndash;0.3%</strong>. The route factor moves it by <strong>3&ndash;48%</strong>. Refining the\n      earth model while quoting a straight line is polishing a rounding error inside a much larger one.\n      The corridor is where the accuracy is.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">02</span> Where each piece lives</h2>\n  <p>The estate already has a working shape: a maths repo with no data, data repos that pin their\n    sources and publish verified products, and consumers that read products and never sources. This\n    scope keeps that shape rather than inventing one.</p>\n\n<pre><span class=\"c\">  source                          derivation                      consumer</span>\n  NESO ETYS 2025      ─────►  data-grid-gb            ─────►  Atlas cartridge\n  (SHA-256 pinned)            connection-points.v3            substation-intelligence\n                              gb-transmission-network\n\n  OSM roads, rail     ─────►  <span class=\"cy\">data-grid-routes</span>        ─────►  <span class=\"cy\">Atlas cartridge</span>\n  (to be pinned)              <span class=\"cy\">corridor-graph.v1</span>              <span class=\"cy\">corridor-intelligence</span>\n                              <span class=\"cy\">routed-distances.v1</span>\n                                     ▲\n                                     │ uses\n                              <span class=\"cy\">grid-distance-maths</span>\n                              geodesy + <span class=\"cy\">routing kernel</span>\n                              no data, dual implementation</pre>\n\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>grid-distance-maths</strong> stays the pure kernel &mdash; no network access, no data files,\n      two independent implementations, parity-tested. Gains a routing module and the stress harness.</li>\n    <li><strong>data-grid-routes</strong> is new and follows the <code>data-*</code> convention exactly: fetch\n      OSM extracts, pin by SHA-256, derive products, verify, publish.</li>\n    <li><strong>corridor-intelligence</strong> is a new Atlas cartridge that reads products and computes nothing\n      it can read. It pins a schema and refuses on mismatch, the way substation-intelligence does.</li>\n  </ul>\n  <p>Nothing in <code>data-grid-gb</code> changes. The corridor engine is additive.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">03</span> Module A &mdash; the maths kernel</h2>\n  <p>Pure functions over coordinates. No fetching, no globals, no knowledge of substations. Everything\n    here is testable without a network and runs identically in Node and Python.</p>\n\n  <div class=\"grid2\">\n    <div>\n      <h3>Already present</h3>\n      <ul>\n        <li><code>distanceKm</code>, <code>distanceEllipsoidalKm</code>, <code>pathLengthKm</code></li>\n        <li><code>initialBearingDeg</code>, <code>destinationPoint</code></li>\n        <li><code>distanceToSegmentKm</code>, <code>distanceToLineKm</code></li>\n        <li><code>geodesicCircle</code>, <code>circleApproximationError</code></li>\n        <li><code>polygonAreaKm2</code>, <code>SpatialIndex</code></li>\n      </ul>\n    </div>\n    <div>\n      <h3>To add</h3>\n      <ul>\n        <li><code>snapToGraph(point, graph, maxKm)</code> &mdash; nearest routable node with the snap distance returned, never hidden</li>\n        <li><code>route(a, b, graph, weights)</code> &mdash; A* with an admissible great-circle heuristic</li>\n        <li><code>crossings(path, barriers)</code> &mdash; segment-intersection counts by barrier class</li>\n        <li><code>corridorLength(path)</code> &mdash; geodesic polyline length, not planar</li>\n        <li><code>routeFactor(path, straight)</code> &mdash; the ratio, reported not applied</li>\n        <li><code>simplify(path, toleranceM)</code> &mdash; geodesic-aware Douglas-Peucker</li>\n      </ul>\n    </div>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">Design rule</div>\n    <p>A snap distance is part of the answer. If a substation is 900 m from the nearest routable road,\n      the route is 900 m short at one end and the card must say so. Silently snapping is how a\n      routing engine starts lying.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">04</span> Module B &mdash; the stress harness</h2>\n  <p>Four independent layers. A geometry bug that survives all four is a bug nobody on this estate\n    could have found by reading.</p>\n\n  <h3>1. Invariants &mdash; property-based, thousands of random cases</h3>\n<pre>identity        d(a,a) = 0\nsymmetry        d(a,b) = d(b,a)                     to 1e-9 relative\ntriangle        d(a,c) &le; d(a,b) + d(b,c)\nbearing round   destination(a, bearing(a,b), d(a,b)) = b\nroute &ge; line    routeKm &ge; straightKm                 always, no exceptions\nroute factor    1.0 &le; factor &le; 10.0                  outside this, fail loudly\npath length     sum of leg lengths = corridorLength(path)\ndeterminism     same input, same output, across both implementations</pre>\n\n  <h3>2. Adversarial cases &mdash; a fixed corpus, not random</h3>\n  <ul>\n    <li>Coincident and near-coincident points (1 mm, 1 cm, 1 m apart)</li>\n    <li>Antipodal and near-antipodal pairs &mdash; where iterative inverse solutions fail to converge</li>\n    <li>The poles, and paths crossing them</li>\n    <li>The antimeridian, in both directions</li>\n    <li>Points either side of the Greenwich meridian and the equator, for sign handling</li>\n    <li>Degenerate graphs: an isolated node, a disconnected component, a zero-length edge</li>\n    <li>A substation with no road within 50 km &mdash; the engine must return <em>no route</em>, not a wrong one</li>\n  </ul>\n\n  <h3>3. Oracles &mdash; independent, external, authoritative</h3>\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>oracle</th><th>what it proves</th><th>tolerance</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">Karney GeodTest</td><td class=\"d\">Geodesic inverse solutions against 500,000 published high-precision cases</td><td>&lt; 1 mm</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">the second implementation</td><td class=\"d\">JS against Python on identical inputs, neither knowing the other's answers</td><td>1e-9 relative</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">published cable circuits</td><td class=\"d\">Routed distance against NESO's own <code>cable_km</code>, n=95</td><td>see below</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">pandapower</td><td class=\"d\">Electrical quantities only, once the engine computes any. BSD-3, cited not bundled.</td><td>per quantity</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n\n  <h3>4. The acceptance test that matters</h3>\n  <div class=\"measured\">\n    <div class=\"lbl\">Self-validating, using data you already publish</div>\n    <p>NESO publishes <code>cable_km</code> for 95 circuits whose endpoints both have coordinates. Those\n      are real buried cable routes with a known built length. <strong>Route between the two substations\n      along the road graph and compare.</strong> The straight line is wrong by a median of 34% on this set.\n      A routed engine that does not beat that is not earning its complexity.</p>\n    <p><strong>Gate:</strong> median absolute error against published <code>cable_km</code> must fall below\n      <strong>15%</strong>, and the routed estimate must beat the straight line on at least\n      <strong>80%</strong> of the 95 circuits. Published as a report, not asserted.</p>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">05</span> Module C &mdash; routing, and the railway question</h2>\n\n  <h3>Following roads already solves most of it</h3>\n  <p>A cable route follows made ground because the wayleave, the trenching and the crossings are all\n    cheaper there. Where a road crosses a railway it does so at an existing bridge or culvert &mdash;\n    infrastructure that already has the crossing solved. So <em>route along roads</em> delivers most of\n    <em>avoid railways</em> for free, and it is why the measured cable factor is 1.34 rather than 1.0.</p>\n\n  <h3>Avoidance is the wrong model; cost is the right one</h3>\n  <p>A hard prohibition makes some routes impossible and others absurd &mdash; a project on the far side\n    of a main line has no route at all. Every crossing is a consent event with a cost and a duration, so\n    the correct structure is a weighted graph where a crossing is expensive rather than forbidden. Set the\n    weight high enough and avoidance falls out; set it to infinity and you get a broken engine.</p>\n\n<pre>weight(edge) = lengthKm\n             + <span class=\"cy\">RAIL_PENALTY_KM</span>     &times; railwayCrossings(edge)\n             + <span class=\"cy\">MOTORWAY_PENALTY_KM</span> &times; motorwayCrossings(edge)\n             + <span class=\"cy\">WATER_PENALTY_KM</span>    &times; watercourseCrossings(edge)\n\n<span class=\"c\">penalties are km-equivalents, published in the product and tunable,\nnever hardcoded in the cartridge. the card reports the crossing COUNT\nas a measurement and the penalty as an assumption, separately.</span></pre>\n\n  <p>Defaults to start from, to be calibrated against the 95 cable circuits rather than believed:\n    rail 3.0 km, motorway 2.0 km, watercourse 1.0 km. If calibration says rail should be 8 km, that is\n    a finding about GB consenting, and worth publishing on its own.</p>\n\n  <h3>Graph size, and why it is precomputed</h3>\n  <div class=\"scroll\"><table>\n    <thead><tr><th>layer</th><th class=\"r\">ways</th><th class=\"r\">vertices</th><th class=\"r\">segments</th><th class=\"r\">raw</th></tr></thead>\n    <tbody>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_primary_roads</td><td class=\"r\">163,790</td><td class=\"r\">1,268,704</td><td class=\"r\">1,104,914</td><td class=\"r\">76.0 MB</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_trunk_roads</td><td class=\"r\">130,228</td><td class=\"r\">978,479</td><td class=\"r\">848,251</td><td class=\"r\">64.4 MB</td></tr>\n      <tr><td class=\"k\">uk_mainline_railways</td><td class=\"r\">89,933</td><td class=\"r\">697,695</td><td class=\"r\">607,762</td><td class=\"r\">52.5 MB</td></tr>\n    </tbody>\n  </table></div>\n  <p>193 MB of GeoJSON is not fetchable per session. Two products solve it, and the first is enough\n    for v2:</p>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong><code>routed-distances.v1</code></strong> &mdash; precomputed offline. For every REPD project,\n      the routed corridor to its nearest N connection points. Roughly 7,680 projects &times; 5 &asymp;\n      <strong>38,400 routes</strong>, minutes of CI, a few MB published. The Atlas reads a routed distance\n      the same way it reads a rating. <em>This is v2.</em></li>\n    <li><strong><code>corridor-graph.v1</code></strong> &mdash; the graph itself, junction-contracted and\n      spatially tiled, typed-array encoded, fetched by tile so an arbitrary click can be routed in the\n      browser. <em>This is v3, and only if v2 proves the value.</em></li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">06</span> What the card says afterwards</h2>\n  <p>The claim changes from a superlative over a subset to a measurement with its uncertainty attached.</p>\n<pre><span class=\"c\">today</span>\n  Nearest 400 kV substation: Cowley Substation &middot; 15.76 km\n\n<span class=\"c\">after</span>\n  Cowley Substation &middot; 15.76 km straight line &middot; <span class=\"cy\">18.9 km routed</span>\n  Route follows classified road for 17.4 km; 1.5 km is unrouted, being\n  the snap at each end. Crosses 1 railway, 0 motorways, 3 watercourses.\n  Route factor 1.20, against a measured 1.08-1.28 for GB circuits of\n  this class (median 1.16, n=290 at 400 kV).\n  Nearest among the 214 of 355 published 400 kV sites that carry\n  coordinates. A route is not a wayleave and not a consent.</pre>\n  <p>Every clause is either a measurement or a stated limit. Nothing asserts connectability, which stays\n    outside what any published appendix can support.</p>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">07</span> Phasing</h2>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P0</span><span class=\"ttl\">Make today's claims true</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; no new geometry until green</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Dedupe transformer counts by record, not winding-end &mdash; 92% of sites currently overstate, 1.90&times; network-wide</li>\n      <li>Split the 34 colliding name keys &mdash; stop stripping <code>ONSHORE</code>, <code>OFFSHORE</code>, <code>EXTENSION</code>, which are the words that distinguish the assets</li>\n      <li>State the coordinate coverage wherever the word <em>nearest</em> appears</li>\n      <li>Pin the cartridge's product fetch to a commit, not <code>main</code></li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P1</span><span class=\"ttl\">Geocode the missing 384</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; 400 kV coverage &ge; 95%</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>384 connection points have no coordinates; 141 of them are 400 kV</li>\n      <li>Sources in order of preference: OSM by improved name join, then the TO's own published asset lists, then manual for the residue</li>\n      <li>Every coordinate carries its provenance and a confidence class. A guessed point is labelled a guess or it is not published</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P2</span><span class=\"ttl\">Kernel and stress harness</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; GeodTest &lt; 1 mm, parity 1e-9</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Routing functions land in <code>grid-distance-maths</code>, both implementations</li>\n      <li>Invariants, adversarial corpus, GeodTest, cross-implementation parity</li>\n      <li>CI fails the build on any divergence &mdash; the existing parity-driver pattern, extended</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P3</span><span class=\"ttl\">data-grid-routes and the graph build</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; cable-circuit error &lt; 15% median</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Pin the OSM extracts by SHA-256, the way the NESO appendices are pinned</li>\n      <li>Build the junction-contracted graph; detect and classify every crossing</li>\n      <li>Calibrate the four penalties against the 95 published cable circuits</li>\n      <li>Publish the calibration report whether or not it flatters the model</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P4</span><span class=\"ttl\">routed-distances.v1 and the cartridge</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">gate &middot; every route reproducible from the product</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Precompute project &times; nearest-N corridors in CI, publish with schema and hash</li>\n      <li><code>corridor-intelligence</code> cartridge reads it, pins the schema, refuses on mismatch</li>\n      <li>Card renders routed distance, crossings, snap distance and coverage together</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"phase\">\n    <div class=\"top\"><span class=\"id\">P5</span><span class=\"ttl\">In-browser routing</span>\n      <span class=\"gate\">only if P4 proves the value</span></div>\n    <ul>\n      <li>Tiled <code>corridor-graph.v1</code>, typed arrays, A* in a worker</li>\n      <li>Routes from an arbitrary click, not only from catalogued projects</li>\n    </ul>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<section>\n  <h2><span class=\"n\">08</span> Where this could go wrong</h2>\n  <ul>\n    <li><strong>OSM road coverage is not uniform.</strong> Primary and trunk only; a substation reached by an\n      unclassified lane will snap badly. The snap distance makes this visible rather than silent, and adding\n      <code>highway=unclassified</code> is a data decision with a size cost, not a code change.</li>\n    <li><strong>A routed distance will be read as a route.</strong> It is a corridor length, not a wayleave, not a\n      consent, not a cost. The card language must carry that as firmly as it already carries\n      <em>&ldquo;a rating is not what is free on the circuit&rdquo;</em>.</li>\n    <li><strong>Calibration on 95 circuits is a small sample.</strong> Report the confidence interval, and expect\n      it to widen for regions with few cable circuits.</li>\n    <li><strong>Overhead lines must never be road-routed.</strong> Their measured factor is 1.13 and they cross\n      open country. Applying the road engine to an OHL question would be a worse answer than the straight line.</li>\n    <li><strong>OSM is ODbL.</strong> Unlike BSD-3 on code, the share-alike obligation reaches derived <em>data</em>.\n      A published derived graph needs its licence position settled before it ships.</li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n<footer>\n  <p><strong>Provenance.</strong> Route factors from 815 ETYS circuits with coordinates at both ends, built length\n    from <code>ohl_km + cable_km</code>. Coverage and collision counts from <code>connection-points.v3.json</code> and\n    <code>gb-transmission-network.v1.json</code>. Graph sizes counted from the committed GeoJSON. NESO sources\n    re-downloaded and confirmed against their pinned SHA-256 on 2026-09-03.</p>\n  <p><strong>Not measured here.</strong> Consenting durations, wayleave costs, land ownership, and anything about\n    whether a project can connect &mdash; none of which any published appendix contains.</p>\n</footer>\n</div>\n"
```json
}
```
